title: Fullbody template review
summary: NH reviews the full body template, which he ran himself for his first three years, and argues it creates more problems than it solves because it forces you to hit every muscle each session. He sets out the right way to run it (compounds plus isolation, heavy/medium/light days, supersets, variations), frequency advice by level, and why he thinks recovery is its weak point.
claims: The more a template forces you to train certain body parts, the less flexibility you have; full body is very restrictive and in his view brings more problems to the surface than it solves
He trained full body for three years when he was starting out
Mistake one: a full body made only of machines is just a machine circuit; machines dictate the path, and two years of it gives minimal gains
Hitting every muscle with one isolation exercise each takes far too long to work as a full body
Mistake two: stacking every compound lift into one day overloads overlapping muscles, especially the lower back, leading to injuries, plateaus and over-fatigue
Compounds alone will not build arms: relying only on presses for triceps and rows/chin-ups for biceps leaves them small; isolation is needed
Every template should be compounds completed by isolation, with most tonnage from compounds and variations of compounds added as volume needs rise
Because full body hits everything every session, you do not need to bench three times a week; rotate bench variations to stay healthy long term
Programs must be realistic and not greedy: too much work wastes time, adds fatigue and can make you regress
Fatigue carries across exercises even for unrelated muscles; by exercise five you underperform, and poor cardio makes the heart and lungs the limiter
Supersetting antagonists or unrelated muscles costs only minimal performance, though in a long full body day the loss grows
Before choosing a template, list exercises you have actually done (not ones you like) as trees of specificity, ordered from most to least specific; the longer the list, the more advanced you are
Full body needs heavy, medium and light days for each muscle, otherwise you either sandbag or hit it too hard every time
Keep heavy, medium and light rep ranges close: heavy 3-6, 2-5 or 3-5; medium 6-10 or 6-12; light 8-10, 8-12 or 8-15; avoid 1-rep heavy days paired with 20-rep light days
A different bench variation on the third day can use the medium rep range, since a variation costs less recovery but still carries over
Full body is often recommended to novices but needs a lot of programming knowledge; novices cannot make all the pieces fit
Novices should avoid a long 3-day full body because they lack the work capacity for two-hour sessions
For novices he prefers full body every day, with one heavy compound per day (bench, squat or deadlift), plus an arms day and an abs/GPP day, and the rest hit lightly
Novices should work shy of their maximum recoverable volume; they progress without pushing hard
A 3-day novice full body can work if each day has one main compound and the rest of the body is hit sparingly
Intermediates do well with full body 3-4 times a week, using heavy/medium/light days in sensible rep ranges
Full body suits advanced lifters best: they understand programming and have the work capacity and focus for long sessions with repeated heavy compounds
He runs a gentleman split because he wants his strength work only at the start of the session; for him volume is king
Full body suits high responders to intensity or people who enjoy intense sessions
If he had to cut below five training days he would struggle, since he is not strong enough to make up lost volume with intensity
For advanced lifters, full body 5-7 days or 1-2 days is very hard; 1-2 day versions usually involve sandbagging or undertraining something
3 full body days is doable for people who like intense sessions; 4 days is the sweet spot
The more days you train per week, the more room you have to manipulate volume and intensity
Doubling every compound pattern in one full body day (two knee flexions, two hinges, two presses each way) is not doable; spread exercises across days and raise intensity on main lifts
Full body depends on supersets: straight sets waste time resting, so fit isolation work into the rest between compounds
Use graded strength work: top set on the day's first pattern, a variation in the 8-12 range next, then e.g. a vertical press, rather than max effort on every pattern
Doubling up heavy squat and hinge in one day does not suit full body because the upper body must be trained too; PPL and upper/lower handle it better
With full body, split hinges and knee flexions across days; use low-impact work like glute-ham raises, hyperextensions and leg curls, which can be supersetted
Full body does not need A/B or mirror days; a 4-day template can repeat itself, and every added rotation complicates it
Exercises late in the session progress least because energy is low; put the least important ones there
Full body is unforgiving of skipped exercises; skipping the last quarter every time undertrains a quarter of the body, so vary the order
If days run too long, add a training day and move the leftover volume there
Cover the body with overlap: squats largely handle the lower body, supersetted with calf raises; bench covers the upper body, with triceps extensions supersetted later
Superset compounds with movements that do not use the same muscles, e.g. triceps work alongside a vertical pull
Recovery is his main objection to full body: it is hard to let muscles recover when you hit them all every session, and getting it wrong leaves you under-recovered for heavy days
A light pump on a muscle between hard sessions can help recovery, but managing it is more art than science
Full body six days a week is not recoverable unless you are a novice with low work capacity; twice a week cannot accumulate enough weekly volume
Recovery is like a pot emptying into the muscle: once it is empty, waiting more days adds nothing for muscle, though tendons may benefit
exercises: full body hits chest every day so variations keep you healthy
knee-flexion work for hamstrings without back load
triceps get too little from bench alone
